summary: The Space Health Management System (SHMS / USYS v2.2.2) is an autonomous onboard crew decision-support and ground telemetry platform featuring a bilingual interface and physical NFC badge-tap role switching. To overcome 22-minute Mars communication latencies and blackouts, SHMS operates entirely onboard via an explainable rules engine and 14 device adapters that unify fragmented physiological data—such as exercise metrics, urine assays, sleep patterns, and ocular pressure—to detect critical health risks like kidney stones and Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). This system is crucial for deep-space exploration as it provides transparent clinical alerts, automated countermeasures like Lower Body Negative Pressure suits, and NASA-grounded preventive health management to ensure crew safety when Earth communication is severed.
details:
Here is the project description as plain text, written from your slides and ready to paste:

Space Health Management System (SHMS) is an onboard health decision-support platform for astronauts on long missions, paired with a telemetry portal for the medical team on the ground. Today an astronaut’s health data is scattered: exercise devices (ARED, T2, CEVIS), urine analysis (UWMS), eye pressure measurements, sleep and nutrition each sit in their own system. SHMS brings 14 of these device sources into one hub and runs 10 cross-source rules over them, so it can notice risks that no single device can see. For example, it links rising urine calcium and low urine volume with heavy resistance exercise to flag kidney-stone risk, then tells the astronaut in plain words what to do: drink more water, aim for more than 2.5 L of urine a day, and start potassium citrate. It also watches for bone loss, dehydration, fatigue, balance problems and SANS, the eye condition caused by fluid shifting toward the head in microgravity. If eye pressure reaches 20.5 mmHg the system warns the crew member, and at 24.0 mmHg it raises an automatic SOS and recommends a lower body negative pressure session to pull fluid back toward the legs.

The system has two views. The Crew View is a simple 8-tab daily guide showing today’s tasks, exercise, energy, water, sleep and eye health. The Lab Team View is a 13-tab portal for researchers, with all-crew triage cards, ocular monitoring, ECG, urine lab results and long-term health records. Because tablets in a spacecraft cabin are shared, users switch between these roles by tapping a physical NFC badge, which takes less than a second.

The main benefit is that everything runs fully onboard. On a Mars mission the one-way radio delay can reach 22 minutes and the signal can drop out completely, so the crew cannot wait for Earth to interpret their data. SHMS gives guidance immediately and queues data packets to sync with the ground when the link returns. In the long term, the intended impact is a unified database that links each countermeasure to the recovery that follows it, so future missions can plan prevention with evidence and intervene earlier.

We built the backend in Python 3.11 with FastAPI, using REST and WebSocket, and covered it with 78 automated pytest tests. The frontend is React and TypeScript built with Vite. The same engine runs on three platforms: in the browser through Pyodide WebAssembly with no server needed, as a Windows desktop app, and as an Android app using Chaquopy, the phone’s NFC reader, and NTAG213 and NTAG215 cards as crew badges. We also use the NASA Open Science Data Repository API with caching and an offline fallback. The interface is available in English and Turkish on every screen.

Our project is creative in three ways. First, it is a “glass-box” system instead of a black-box AI: every alert comes with a “Why” trace showing the baseline, trend and statistics behind it, so a stressed astronaut can trust it. Second, the physical NFC badge makes role switching instant and natural. Third, the demo includes a panel where anyone can switch the link between ISS, Gateway and Mars delay, force a communications blackout, or inject a sudden eye-pressure spike and watch the system respond.

Our team considered usability under stress, trust in automated advice, communication delay, privacy and scientific honesty. No real astronaut medical records are used; all data is simulated and labelled “Simulated data” on every screen. Thresholds taken from published NASA research are marked as verified, while 104 model parameters we could not confirm are clearly tagged as unverified.
